2
What Is Image Recognition?
Image recognition is the ability of a computer to identify what an image contains, such as an object, a face or a handwritten digit.
  • Input: an image made of pixels
  • Process: extract features and compare
  • Output: a class label, for example “Apple”
3
From Image to Feature Vector
A computer cannot compare pictures by meaning, so each image is converted into a list of numbers called a feature vector.
1. Image
Photo of a fruit, stored as thousands of pixels
2. Feature extraction
Measure colour, texture, shape or edges
3. Feature vector
For example: (redness 7, roughness 4)
Key idea: images with similar features lie close together in feature space.
4
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
KNN is a supervised machine learning algorithm. It labels a new item by looking at the K most similar labelled examples and taking a majority vote.
K
Number of neighbors
How many close examples are allowed to vote
d
Distance
How similarity is measured; smaller means more alike
✔
Majority vote
The most common class among the neighbors wins
KNN is a “lazy learner”: it stores the training data and does its work at prediction time.
5
How KNN Classifies an Image
1
Collect data
Gather images with known labels
2
Extract features
Convert every image into a vector
3
Choose K
Often a small odd number such as 3 or 5
4
Measure distance
Compare the new image with all stored images
5
Find neighbors
Sort distances and keep the K smallest
6
Vote
Assign the majority class to the new image
6
Measuring Similarity: Distance
Euclidean distance
d = √[ (x₁ − x₂)² + (y₁ − y₂)² ]
For n features: add the squared difference of every feature, then take the square root.
Euclidean
Straight-line distance; the most common choice
Manhattan
Sum of absolute differences between features
Cosine
Compares direction; popular for deep image features

10
Choosing the Value of K
Small K
Example: K = 1
Very sensitive to noise and wrong labels; may overfit.
Balanced K
Found by testing
Try several values on validation data and keep the most accurate one.
Large K
Example: K = all
Boundary becomes too smooth; the largest class tends to win.
Tips: use an odd K for two classes to avoid ties, and scale features so that no single one dominates the distance.
11
Real-World Applications
Handwritten digits
Reading numbers on postal codes and forms
Face recognition
Matching a face to the closest stored face features
Medical imaging
Helping doctors compare scans with labelled cases
Agriculture
Sorting fruit and spotting leaf diseases
Quality control
Detecting defective products in factories
Visual search
Finding products that look like a photo
KNN is one possible method for these tasks, often combined with stronger feature extractors.
12
Advantages and Limitations
Advantages
  • Simple to understand and implement
  • Almost no training time
  • Works for two or many classes
  • New examples can be added easily
Limitations
  • Slow prediction on large datasets
  • Needs memory to store all data
  • Sensitive to irrelevant or unscaled features
  • Weak on raw pixels in high dimensions
13
Conclusion
Images become numbers
Feature representations let a computer measure how similar two images are.
Neighbors decide the class
KNN labels a new image by the majority vote of its K closest examples.
Good features matter most
Meaningful, well-scaled features and a tested K give better results.
